strengths: Addresses genuine gap: De-anonymized observability dataset with scale information is novel and fills a clear need missing from BOOM and other datasets
Comprehensive data collection: Well-designed experimental setup with multiple environmental conditions (3 zones), realistic traffic patterns, and controlled adversarial scenarios (jamming)
Principled anomaly curation: Grounded in technical literature with 8 function types for realistic anomaly manifestation and human-in-the-loop verification
Excellent documentation: Extensive appendices provide procedures, KPI specifications, prompts, and training details that facilitate reproducibility
Multi-modal downstream tasks: Supports anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and question-answering—all practically relevant beyond forecasting
Comprehensive benchmarking: Thorough evaluation of LLMs, reasoning models, foundation models, and traditional time series architectures
Fine-grained temporal resolution: 100ms sampling captures abrupt dynamics characteristic of observability data
Clear presentation: Well-organized with informative figures comparing heterogeneity and resolution of existing datasets
weaknesses: CRITICAL: No explicit statement about dataset release, license, or accessibility—essential information for a dataset paper that is missing
Extremely low anomaly detection precision (0.05-0.3) raises unaddressed questions: Is task ill-posed? Are labels noisy? Is evaluation flawed?
Most anomalies are synthetic (90k) vs. real jamming (30k); no analysis comparing model performance on real vs. synthetic anomalies or validating synthetic realism
Ecological validity concerns: Single lab-controlled 5G environment not representative of operational networks; findings may not generalize to other domains/protocols
Scale information finding underexplored: Only Mantis model preserves scale; no ablation studies comparing normalization strategies or identifying which scale aspects matter most
Limited methodological novelty: Data curation via transformations and LLM prompting is straightforward; no new methods/models proposed
Small evaluation sets: Anomaly detection uses 1,000 samples; question-answering limited to 64 time series + 5 network Q&A; no cross-validation
Missing comparisons: No empirical comparison with BOOM dataset, transfer learning experiments, or ablations on design choices
Question-answering task limitations: Only LLMs evaluated (not time series models); huge variance in difficulty (35%-98% accuracy); limited failure analysis
Synthetic anomaly quality unclear: Parameter ranges suggested by GPT-4.1; human verification mentioned but not detailed (sample size, agreement metrics)

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Observability datasets are scarce and proprietary; de-anonymized data with preserved scale information is valuable for the community

Comprehensive and transparent data curation: Controlled zones, mobility patterns, congestion scenarios, real jamming-based anomalies, and 10 well-motivated synthetic anomaly types with detailed documentation (Algorithm 1, full prompts)
Multi-modal support: Combines time series with natural language (troubleshooting tickets, Q&A pairs), extending beyond typical forecasting-only benchmarks
Scale-aware evaluation: Demonstrates that scale information matters—Mantis (which embeds scale) substantially outperforms other models, highlighting an under-studied but practically important aspect
Rigorous documentation: Extensive appendices with collection procedures, KPI specifications, prompts, network topology, enabling reasonable reproducibility of data collection methodology
weaknesses: Lab-based data severely limits real-world applicability: Collected from controlled lab 5G network, not operational infrastructure. No evidence that observed dynamics (error patterns, failure modes) generalize to real telecom networks, undermining practical value despite addressing a real gap

Synthetic anomalies methodology concerns: 70% of anomalies are synthetic (generated via GPT-4.1 parameter ranges + human validation). Validation process poorly described (number of validators, inter-rater agreement not reported), creating LLM circularity risk since LLM-generated anomalies are evaluated with LLMs. Critically, no breakdown of model performance on real vs. synthetic anomalies separately

Benchmarking reveals predictable results without actionable insights: Main findings (erratic observability data causes false positives in anomaly detection, LLMs struggle) are unsurprising. Scale information matters (Mantis result) is valuable but lacks ablation studies. Anomaly detection evaluated on only 1,000 samples; no statistical significance testing. Forecasting section contradicts motivation that forecasting is not critical

Limited scope and generalization: Single technology (5G wireless only), single environment (lab), single domain (telecommunications). No infrastructure, database, or security observability. Unclear if dataset will be released publicly—critical unresolved issue for dataset papers; significantly reduces reproducibility and community impact

Insufficient evaluation rigor: No inter-annotator agreement metrics for synthetic anomaly validation. No error analysis explaining high variance in QA results (MAE 0.163–1588.1). Missing ablations isolating effects of scale preservation. QA performance inconsistent (some tasks ~76% accuracy, others chance-level), unexplained. Evaluation methodology underdeveloped compared to benchmarking breadth

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in observability datasets with careful experimental design; de-anonymization and scale preservation improve over prior work like BOOM
Exemplary documentation with Algorithm 1, complete prompts, and detailed appendices enabling reproducibility and verification
Comprehensive benchmarking across diverse model families (LLMs, reasoning models, foundation models, time series architectures) with appropriate metrics
Principled synthetic anomaly generation grounded in telecom literature with expert review and realistic effect functions
Multi-modal capability (time series + language QA) is novel for observability and enables evaluation of multi-modal reasoning
Valuable finding about importance of scale-aware designs (e.g., Mantis) for observability tasks
Heterogeneous data types (categorical, integers, floats with diverse ranges, 100ms resolution) reflect real operational systems
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Paper does not state whether dataset will be publicly released, essential for impact and reproducibility of a dataset contribution
Limited to single domain (5G telecom); generalization to cloud systems, data centers, or other observability domains unclear
Lab-controlled environment with artificially induced anomalies (jamming) rather than production data; real anomalies may manifest differently
Primarily diagnostic rather than prescriptive: demonstrates model failures but lacks ablation studies, mechanistic analysis, or proposed improvements
Missing statistical rigor: no significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; no inter-rater agreement metrics for human verification steps
Synthetic anomaly parameters generated by GPT-4.1 with human validation but no quantified quality metrics or systematic bias analysis
Categorical variables oversold: only 2 categorical KPIs with most values being 'none'; claims of heterogeneity somewhat overstated
No direct empirical comparison with BOOM dataset, the main related work mentioned throughout
Class imbalance: 95-5 normal-anomalous ratio maintained based on existing benchmarks despite potential mismatch with real networks; sensitivity unexplored
Question-answering task limited: only 4 LLMs evaluated; reasoning models and multimodal models untested; no analysis of QA difficulty or coverage

strengths: Well-motivated contribution addressing a clear gap: observability data is underrepresented in ML benchmarks due to proprietary restrictions, yet exhibits unique characteristics (zero-inflation, high variance, minimal temporal structure) distinct from climate/finance time series

Comprehensive and principled dataset construction: Real 5G network with controlled experiments, systematic data collection across zones/traffic types/mobility conditions, careful multi-source alignment using histogram-based KL matching, and mixed real (jammer-induced) and synthetic anomalies grounded in telecommunications literature

Novel dataset properties: De-anonymized covariates preserving absolute scale information (major advantage over BOOM), heterogeneous mixed-type metrics (10 float, 6 integer, 2 categorical), and multi-modal downstream tasks with explicit reasoning traces for interpretability

Extensive benchmarking across diverse model families (LLMs, reasoning models, time series architectures, foundation models) revealing consistent failure patterns and systematic model underperformance on observability tasks

Strong empirical insight on scale information: Table 7 ablation convincingly demonstrates scale is critical, with gains up to 41.1 points on root cause identification, highlighting a key failure mode in normalized observability datasets
Thorough documentation with comprehensive appendices covering data collection algorithms, anomaly curation methodology, prompt engineering, and KPI specifications to facilitate reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited scope undermines generalizability claims: Single 5G network in controlled 70m² lab with 3 zones, one vendor (OpenAirInterface), single device type—yet paper positions this as general 'observability' dataset relevant to 'complex systems'. No data from databases, cloud platforms, or distributed systems. Telecommunications-specific findings may not transfer to other observability domains despite implicit universality claims

Synthetic anomaly quality concerns: Only 10 anomaly types insufficient for real-world diversity; heavy reliance on GPT-4.1 for troubleshooting tickets without human validation of synthetic anomalies themselves; soft-bound thresholds at 20th percentile set arbitrarily without sensitivity analysis; missing inter-annotator agreement for anomaly realism

Evaluation protocol limitations: Anomaly detection evaluation uses only 1,000 randomly selected samples (acknowledged due to 'computational cost')—may not be representative; forecasting acknowledges MAE inappropriate for observability data (Appendix H) but proposes no alternative metrics; no statistical significance testing; no inter-rater agreement for reasoning traces

Reasoning trace fidelity concerns: Traces generated with ground-truth labels as conditioning—may not reflect realistic reasoning without label access; scoring function (Eq. 1-3) uses hand-crafted regex patterns and weighted combinations appearing ad hoc; best-selected traces have mean score 0.75 only; metadata leakage prevention via informal 'lexical blacklists' lacks empirical validation of leakage rates

Insufficient scale analysis: 32K samples with ~2.2M Q&A likely template-generated with high redundancy; no comparison to pretraining corpus sizes for existing models (Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai); unclear if sufficient for pretraining observability-specific foundation models; no analysis of label distributions or task difficulty

Privacy and ethics under-addressed: De-anonymization creates privacy risks not discussed; 'Impact Statement' is dismissive ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted'); no discussion of dual-use risks (patterns enabling adversarial attacks on real 5G); no IRB approval mentioned

Limited methodological novelty: Primarily dataset curation without new modeling techniques; multi-modal model (Toto+Qwen-3-4B) uses straightforward early-fusion; scale ablation adds scaling branch ad hoc rather than exploring native scale-aware architectures

Incomplete technical transparency: Synthetic anomaly parameter ranges ('feasible values' from GPT-4.1) not reported; hyperparameter selection for benchmarked models minimal (Appendix G); many arbitrary design choices (100ms resolution, 128-step windows, stride-32) without justification; no sensitivity analyses

Presentation issues: 31 pages with heavy appendices; Figures 7-12 comparing datasets repetitive; Section 2 comparison to BOOM lacks quantitative details; key methodological details should be in main text; 'multi-modal' framing slightly oversold (early-fusion is standard)

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: First large-scale de-anonymized observability dataset with preserved scale information, filling a real need in the community
Comprehensive curation: Thoughtful combination of real anomalies (controlled jamming) and literature-grounded synthetic anomalies with explicit reasoning traces
Scale information validation: Section 4.6 provides solid empirical evidence of scale importance through ablation studies with concrete improvements (up to 41 points)
Detailed dataset comparison: Appendix A systematically demonstrates heterogeneity and characteristics unique to TelecomTS vs. existing time series datasets
Broad task coverage: Multi-modal downstream tasks spanning anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and question-answering beyond typical forecasting benchmarks
Thorough methodology documentation: Detailed appendices on data collection, network setup, anomaly curation, and evaluation procedures
weaknesses: Critical testbed limitation: Data from controlled lab environment (~70 m²) not production networks; claims about 'real-world observability' are undermined by artificial conditions (single base station, 18 KPIs, controlled jamming)

Limited novelty for ICML main track: Primarily dataset curation without methodological innovation, algorithmic contributions, or theoretical insights; benchmarking applies existing models without adaptation
Narrow domain scope: Exclusively 5G telecommunications with no generalization studies to other observability domains (cloud infrastructure, databases); generalizability is unexplored

Problematic reasoning trace generation: Traces generated by conditioning LLMs on ground-truth labels and metadata (though claimed not exposed at inference); lacks independent human validation, undermining supervision signal quality

Unexplained experimental findings: Multi-modal models underperform unimodal baselines (Table 4), large performance variance across tasks (0.400 to 0.992 for same model in Table 6); no investigation of contradictions

Evaluation methodology gaps: Small test set (1K samples) for anomaly detection, no temporal leakage analysis for sliding window construction, missing statistical significance tests and confidence intervals

Synthetic anomaly validation: Split between real/synthetic anomalies not quantified, no analysis of synthetic anomaly diversity vs. real failures, no performance comparison on real vs. synthetic anomalies
Reproducibility concerns: Specialized 5G infrastructure difficult to reproduce, unclear what code/data is released, complex tuning steps documented only in appendices
Limited experimental insights: Findings (models struggle with noisy data, scale matters, LLMs fail at time series) are mostly expected observations rather than novel discoveries
Venue mismatch: Better suited for datasets track or networking/observability domain venue; lacks research contribution depth expected for ICML main track

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: first publicly available de-anonymized observability dataset with absolute scale information and multi-modal tasks, filling a critical need in the time series benchmarking landscape

Rigorous and well-documented data collection: comprehensive 5G testbed with spatial zoning, diverse traffic scenarios, controlled jamming for real anomalies, and detailed synchronization procedures enabling full reproducibility
Principled anomaly curation combining real and synthetic anomalies grounded in telecommunications literature with 8 different effect functions and human-in-the-loop validation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse model families (LLMs, reasoning models, time series models, multi-modal models) revealing consistent performance gaps and systematic challenges
Compelling evidence for core motivation: scale ablation study (Table 7) demonstrates 20-30+ point improvements across architectures, with Autoformer gaining 30.4 points on root cause analysis

Exceptional reproducibility: extensive appendices with all KPI definitions, prompts, training details, Algorithm 1 for data collection procedures, and structured metadata examples enabling community reproduction
Multi-modal reasoning traces with automatic quality-scoring function and metadata leakage prevention provide valuable supervision signals for reasoning-capable models
Clear, honest treatment of limitations including forecasting challenges (Appendix H) and testbed constraints, demonstrating methodological maturity
weaknesses: Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests across any results; unclear if results are from single runs or multiple trials; only 1K samples used for anomaly detection with justification limited to computational constraints

Critical methodological details underspecified: train/test split strategy (random vs. temporal) not clarified; hyperparameter tuning equity not discussed; frozen backbone evaluation may handicap foundation models; 80/20 anomaly prevalence is artificial without reporting natural prevalence

Testbed limitations reduce real-world applicability: controlled lab environment (~70 m²), single base station, single user equipment cannot capture multi-user interference or large-scale operational complexity despite claims of generalizability

Scope limited to 5G telecommunications: generalization to other observability domains (cloud systems, databases, IoT) unclear; no validation on real operational network data to verify synthetic setup representativeness

Reasoning trace quality relies solely on automatic scoring without human validation: scoring function weights (0.50, 0.30, 0.20) lack justification; potential for implicit information leakage through ground-truth conditioning not thoroughly explored; Figure 17 shows score distributions but lacks detailed qualitative analysis

Incremental experimental insights: findings that LLMs struggle with anomaly detection and models fail on bursty data are somewhat expected; limited failure analysis (single example in Figure 6); no confusion matrices for root cause analysis showing which fault types are confused

No proposed solutions: paper identifies problems effectively but offers limited architectural guidance beyond 'add scale encoding'; could include more specific recommendations for practitioners on normalization strategies or threshold selection
Time Series Q&A limited to basic statistics (mean, variance, periodicity, trend): falls short of true temporal reasoning; missing analysis of which KPI characteristics make tasks hard

Critical missing details: network synchronization error bounds for histogram-matching not validated; sensitivity to key design choices (sample length 128, stride 32) not analyzed; no quantitative comparison with BOOM on overlapping tasks despite it being primary related work
